units: a fitness coach notices that beginners are out of breath after a single flight of stairs
a seated life weakens the breath without drawing attention
the heart muscle gets used to reduced effort
the vessels become less elastic
nightly rest deteriorates in bodies that are rarely worked
the coach advises brisk walks repeated during the week
those walks include moderate climbs
late-afternoon weariness lessens once this habit is kept
text: At a neighborhood gym, a trainer watches the door. Newcomers come in winded, and all they have done is climb one flight of stairs. He knows the pattern well. A seated life wears down the machinery of breathing quietly, never announcing itself. Sit still for months and the heart muscle settles for very little work, while the vessels stiffen and lose their spring, so that any short run turns punishing. There is a quieter cost too. Sleep frays, because a body that asks nothing of itself never earns deep repair. His remedy is a modest one: brisk walks, several times a week, with a few moderate climbs worked into the route. The change shows up fast. Breathing stretches out, the late-afternoon slump loosens its grip, and the mood clears. Nothing dramatic here, only an ordinary cause, an ordinary correction, a chain that runs backward.

units: evenings are taken over by bright screens
falling asleep is pushed later and later
the writer refuses to blame the devices themselves
the writer blames the lack of a limit set in advance
he recommends choosing a stopping hour before the evening
he advises leaving the device outside the bedroom
he suggests replacing that habit with quiet reading
he claims that a gentle rule is what makes it last
text: Our evenings have filled with bright screens until they overflow. After dark the eye catches on a cold glow, thought thins out inside it, and sleep slides back half an hour, then half an hour more. I distrust the easy accusation. The harm does not live in the device. It lives in the missing boundary, the one nobody drew before tiredness stripped away our judgment. A blunt ban would fail, the way severe diets fail. What I defend is a calmer arrangement, negotiated with oneself. Pick the stopping hour at midday, while the mind is still clear. Leave the device outside the bedroom, so that reaching for it costs something. Put a slow book, a low conversation, a long stretch where the electric vigil used to sit. Sleep is never rescued by heroic denial, only by a mild rule you keep without thinking about it.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a rehabilitation therapist has worked with back patients since the start of his career
he contrasts two profiles among the people he sees
the first profile carries heavy loads and has tight musculature
the second profile stays seated and lacks muscle tone
both profiles complain of a comparable discomfort
he treats the first with stretching and heat
he treats the second with gradual strengthening
he refuses to apply the same protocol to both cases
text: The therapist in this practice has spent his whole working life on backs, and he sorts every patient into one of two groups before examining anyone. The first hauls weight for a good part of the week. The muscles come in tight, the shoulders locked, the neck hard under the palm. The second sits at a screen all day. The tissue is slack, the posture caves inward, the belly wall holds nothing up any more. Both describe the same ache low in the spine, which is why people assume one treatment would serve them equally. He says the opposite. For the first he orders slow stretching, heat, and release guided by the breath, until a clenched back moves freely again. For the second he sets out gradual strengthening, and without it no relief lasts. One symptom, he says, hiding two opposite machines.

units: a cookery book meant for people recovering from illness is examined
the reviewer approves of the plainness of the preparations
the recipes limit fats and long cooking
the book offers combinations rich in protein
the portions are suited to a weakened appetite
the explanations about chewing are judged useful
the review faults the absence of any guidance on keeping food
the closing lines recommend the book to family kitchens all the same
text: This collection of dishes written for people recovering from illness deserves close attention, since its choices cut against nearly everything the genre produces. Restraint comes first. The author drops the endless braises and the heavy fats in favor of plates a weakened stomach accepts without protest. Then come the pairings, each one built around a protein source, so that a meal sustains rather than crushes. The servings, too, are cut back to what a faded appetite can honestly face. And the pages on chewing are worth more than several longer treatises. One reservation remains. Nothing is said about keeping dishes that were made ahead of time, a regrettable gap for readers with little strength to spare. Even so, the book belongs in any household kitchen where somebody is getting well again.

units: the writer of the message sends news to someone close
a chill came on at the end of the week
a consultation took place the following day
the nurse ruled out any complication
an extended rest of three nights was prescribed
a hot drink and a light soup made up the whole diet
the fever dropped before the treatment was over
the writer promises a visit as soon as he is well
text: I am writing to you from bed, and there is nothing here that should worry you. It all began at the end of the week. A chill caught me while I was tidying the kitchen, and I went down feverish, incapable of finishing my own sentence. The following day the nurse at the clinic nearby examined me thoroughly. She ruled out any complication and prescribed three nights of strict rest, which I accepted without argument. The first two dragged. Nothing went down except warm tea and a thin soup, and I fell asleep the moment the light went out. Then the fever broke abruptly, before the course was even finished, and my hunger returned like a friend who had walked off in a temper. I can cross the hallway now without leaning on the wall. I will visit as soon as this tiredness releases me.

units: the person being asked explains night sweating
an overheated bedroom prevents the inner temperature from falling
that fall is what allows proper sleep to begin
the body makes up for it by producing sweat
wakings multiply because of that discomfort
the next day's tiredness follows from those interruptions
the woman answering advises turning down the heat in the bedroom
she recommends natural fabrics rather than synthetic ones
text: You want to know why your pillow is drenched every night although you have exerted yourself in no way. Short answer: your bedroom is overheated. Here is what happens. To drop off properly, your body must let its own temperature fall by a fraction of a degree, and if the surrounding air prevents that, it brings out the heavy machinery and makes you perspire. So what? So you surface clammy, shove the blanket off, drag it back, and that whole performance chops your night into useless fragments. That is where the heavy morning comes from, although you never stayed up late. What should you actually do? Turn the heating down well before bed and let the room cool by itself. Swap the bedding too. Natural fabrics let the damp escape, synthetics trap it against your skin. Give it a week and see.

units: an intake nurse describes the crowding in an emergency department
most of the arrivals involve complaints of no seriousness
seriously ill patients wait longer because of that crowding
a senior doctor points to ignorance about the options available
a telephone line for guidance has been set up
walk-in appointments open in the evening
average waiting time has fallen since these measures
the nurse holds that informing the public must go on
text: The nurse on intake describes a waiting room that is full before the doors have properly opened. Most of the people in it, she says, have come with something inconsequential, a mild sprain, a cough that refuses to clear, a shallow burn, and those files push the genuinely threatened patients back down the queue. The senior doctor agrees, with a qualification. People rarely know what exists outside the hospital, he explains, so they head for the building they can name. Two measures followed. A telephone line now sorts callers before anyone sets off, and walk-in evening clinics have opened around the district. Average waiting time has already fallen, he notes. The nurse remains more guarded about it. The room empties for good only once everyone knows where to turn, and not a day sooner.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the healers of the past put illness down to tainted air
they advised airing rooms out and keeping away from unhealthy places
that explanation rested on observation without proof
the discovery of micro-organisms changed that view
handwashing was brought into the care wards
deaths after childbirth fell afterwards
both approaches shared the same distrust of dirt
the older approach knew nothing of the true source of contagion
text: Before anyone could look at the invisible, healers laid the blame on the air. A thick smell rising off a marsh, an alley with no draft, a shut room: that, people believed, was where contagion came from. So they opened windows, burned herbs, and kept away from the low quarters. The instinct was not foolish. It was simply blind to its own reason. Then curved glass revealed a minute population swarming across the fingers, and the whole picture turned over. An unremarkable instruction, wash your hands between one ward and the next, brought down deaths among women who had just given birth as no smoke ever had. Set the two doctrines honestly side by side. Each mistrusted filth, and each prescribed much the same gestures. But the older one aimed at a shadow, while the newer could finally name what it was fighting.

units: the text describes what happens when the body is plunged into cold water
the skin reacts by tightening the vessels near the surface
the blood pulls back toward the organs at the core
breathing speeds up sharply on contact
controlling the breath limits that reaction
stimulating substances are released after coming out
heart trouble is a reason not to take it up
a short spell is advised for beginners
text: Going into cold water works on three separate levels, and each one is worth taking apart on its own. Circulation comes first. On contact the vessels just under the skin clamp down, the blood pulls back toward the organs at the core, and pressure climbs for a short while. Breathing follows. A reflex gasp arrives the instant you go under, fast and outside your control, and steadying the out-breath softens that panic and makes the whole thing workable. Last comes the chemical answer. Once you climb out, the body releases stimulating messengers, which is what regular swimmers mean when they call it bracing. Two limits frame all of it. Any known heart trouble rules the practice out without medical advice, and a beginner keeps the immersion very short, never alone, never on a full stomach.

units: a librarian suffered from pain in her wrists
she first put that pain down to her age
a colleague pointed out the unsuitable height of her work surface
an ergonomist examined her workstation
the chair and the screen were raised
regular breaks were brought into her day
the pain went away after several weeks
she then urged the same approach on her colleagues
text: The head of the town library endured a dull ache in both wrists for the better part of two seasons, and she put it down to her age and to ordinary wear. She went on shelving, carrying, typing out references, until a younger colleague remarked on the odd height of the sorting counter she worked at. An ergonomist was called in. He measured the station, watched how her forearms sat, and gave his verdict without softening it: the chair was too low, the screen too far back, and the neck was paying for the whole imbalance. Both were raised. Short breaks were written into the day at fixed intervals. Some weeks later the ache had gone, and not one tablet had been swallowed. From then on she preached the same procedure to her staff, with a stubbornness nobody could talk her out of.
